title: 1999 HMMT February Advanced Topics Problem 3
statement: An unfair coin has the property that when flipped four times, it has the same probability of turning up 2 heads and 2 tails (in any order) as 3 heads and 1 tail (in any order). What is the probability of getting a head in any one flip?

solutions.text: Let \(p\) be the probability of getting a head in one flip. There are 6 ways to get 2 heads and 2 tails, each with probability \(p^{2}(1-p)^{2}\), and 4 ways to get 3 heads and 1 tail, each with probability \(p^{3}(1-p)\). We are given that \(6 p^{2}(1-p)^{2}=4 p^{3}(1-p)\). Clearly \(p\) is not 0 or 1 , so we can divide by \(p^{2}(1-p)\) to get \(6(1-p)=4 p\). Therefore \(p\) is \(\frac{3}{5}\).
